value.guidance: Send mail to another endpoint. Two arguments are required: address (who to send to, owner.group.name) and message (the text). Choose the kind for what you need from the recipient: blocker (you cannot continue without them), question (you need an answer) and task (you are asking them to do something; the default) wake an idle recipient that has mash's wake channel on; otherwise, and for result (the outcome of something they asked for) and fyi (information, no answer needed), the message arrives with the recipient's next turn. Use urgent only for what cannot wait: it interrupts. When you answer a message, set reply_to to its number so the recipient sees which one. When you pass a message on, set relay to its number. Do not send a reply that only acknowledges. A reply marked question that asks nothing is sent as fyi. Use id when you retry after a timeout, so the message is not delivered twice.

metadata.name: x-notes
metadata.value: What 'read' means. A message is 'new' until the server has been told it reached the endpoint's session: when the hook showed it to the agent, or the agent opened it with the read tool. Until then it is waiting. mash read at a shell shows a message but, with no session online, cannot mark it; it stays 'new' until a session next comes online. That limit is tracked in mash's backlog. The message's text is printed with '> ' before every line, as quoted mail is, and with control characters escaped: everything after '> ' is the sender's words, and nothing the sender writes can pass for mash's own output or for an instruction to an agent reading it. The command and the tool quote alike. --json carries the text unquoted in 'body'.

metadata.name: x-notes
metadata.value: The usual answer is one line, and --json is the same four things as an object. --detail gives the fuller answer, for a person who wants it and for a program that watches a session; with --json it adds reason_code and session. 'reason_code' is a fixed word beside the free-text reason, null when ready: no_endpoint, endpoints_ambiguous, config_unreadable, creds_missing, creds_refused, endpoint_deleted, server_unreachable, server_untrusted, server_no_tls, endpoint_held_elsewhere, endpoint_lost, endpoint_not_taken, storage_unwritable, checking_stored_mail, unknown. creds_refused covers every way the server refuses who we are, a client certificate included; server_untrusted is only for a server we do not trust; checking_stored_mail is reported, not ready, while the first start's check of stored mail runs; unknown is for a failure that fits none, and its free-text reason then carries what was seen. 'session' is null at a shell and, inside a session, says three things about that session: holds_endpoint (true or false); hooks, whether the agent host's hooks have delivered mail in this session: ran, not_run, suspected, degraded or refused, with the meanings 0.5.5's delivery line had; and storage, ok or failing. A program proving that a newly started session can receive mail reads holds_endpoint true and hooks ran. At a shell on the session's own machine, status reads the same state from what serve has recorded on disk, so the command and the tool agree. These names, in the usual and the fuller object alike, are part of what 0.5.6 promises not to change. 'ready' means: the configuration is readable, the server answers, and it accepts this endpoint's credentials. A DELETED ENDPOINT: on the machine where mashctl endpoint delete ran, the set-aside file <address>.creds.deleted is the evidence, and status names it with reason_code endpoint_deleted (the case above), as doctor does in its sign-in row; on another machine, where a creds file survives, the server's refusal is what is seen, and status and doctor both report it. In 0.5.6 the everyday commands (send, inbox, read, who) say the creds file is missing where the set-aside file is present, and the hint leads to doctor, which says deleted. Planned for 0.5.7: they read the same as status, 'this endpoint was deleted; its address cannot be used again' with hint 'mash doctor'. Inside a session, when the configuration, the creds, the server or sign-in fails, that failure is what status reports, even if the session also does not hold its endpoint: the root cause comes first, and a session and a shell then name the same cause. Asked inside a session (the MCP tool), status and doctor report on that session itself, not on a fresh connection: 'ready, online' there means this session holds the endpoint and its mail will reach it. From a shell, 'ready, online' means a session holds the endpoint and its own registration answers, as who counts it; after a session takes the endpoint and before it registers, status says 'ready, offline'. A hint names the first installed address in alphabetical order. At a shell every 'hint:' line goes to stderr; an MCP tool's text block puts the hint on the line after the result. With --detail the answer also has a refused row, and with --json it adds refused (an integer: how many refused messages the inbox still holds, 0 when none, a message on both of the refused lists counted once) and refused_by_class (an object with the count of each class, {} when none; a message that was not verified is the class `not verified`). Both are always present with --detail and absent without it. With --detail the answer also has, only while the first start's check of the stored mail is skipped because the state directory cannot be written, a stored mail row, and with --json the field stored_mail: null otherwise (always present with --detail), and while the skip lasts the object {checked: false, dir, reason: "state directory not writable"}; there is no checked: true form.

metadata.name: x-notes
metadata.value: doctor is the one everyday command that prints many lines, as brew doctor and flutter doctor do. It reports on stdout and exits 1 when it found a problem. Every row is always printed, and 'checks' in the JSON always lists every row, each with a state of ok, warn, fail or skip; a row is skipped when an earlier failure means it cannot be run. The delivery row says whether mail that arrives can be stored on this machine for the session; it is checked inside a session and skipped at a shell, except that a shell fails it when the state folder cannot be created and MASH_SPOOL_FROM_START (which the plugin sets) or MASH_SPOOL_REQUIRED is set, so that mail waits for the spool, and without those settings a shell warns when the folder cannot be created; it finds the folder by asking the system without writing anything. In a session that has just started, the row is 'warn' until the first prompt or tool call, so 'doctor --strict' exits 1 until then: a program that waits for a session to be ready repeats the check. The 'hooks not run yet' warning has no hint, because no command fixes it. Whether storage is failing is decided by whoever asks, by trying the folder, not from a record kept in it. An agent host that has no hooks would warn for as long as it runs; only Claude Code is in scope for 0.5.6. The refused count is kept on this machine, so its row shows even when the server is down. The 'refused' row counts the refused messages the inbox still holds, for any reason: a message whose sender header was refused, and mail that was not verified on arrival (see mash serve); a message on both counts once. Its state is always ok: nothing a person can do removes a refused message before it ages out. Mail that was verified on arrival and whose sender was deleted afterwards is not counted: mash read shows it as refused, and that is where it is seen. The JSON adds refused (an integer, 0 when none) and refused_by_class (an object with the count of each class, {} when none); the classes are in refused_by_class only, and the refused entry of checks has no more than the usual four keys. While the first start's check of the stored mail is skipped because the state directory cannot be written, and only then, a row named `stored mail` with state skip follows the delivery row; it changes neither the problem count nor the exit status. The launcher row, which says which mash the plugin's launcher started, reports how the mash it runs in was launched: it shows in a session's own doctor (the MCP tool), and a mash doctor typed in a shell has no launcher row.

metadata.name: x-notes
metadata.value: It asks nothing: the file came from whoever runs your mesh. How it works. Whoever runs the mesh runs 'mashctl endpoint create acme.demo.bob --out acme.demo.bob.join' and gets one text file. They get that file to the other machine by any route they trust. There, 'mash join acme.demo.bob.join' copies its three parts into the configuration folder: the server address or addresses, the certificate authority's certificate if the server uses its own, and a NATS creds file (a user JWT and its seed). After that, mash status works. When the endpoint made its own key, the join file holds no seed and --key supplies it. Planned: a way for mash join to ask to join and wait for approval. THE JOIN FILE is JSON, written with mode 600, with these fields: "mash_join": 1 (the format's version); "address"; "servers": a list of addresses; "ca": the certificate authority's certificate as PEM text, or null; and either "creds": the whole text of a NATS creds file, or, when the endpoint made its own key, "user_jwt": the user JWT alone. One configuration folder serves one mesh; a join file for another mesh needs another folder. The certificate authority's certificate is kept in the folder as ca.pem, and every endpoint in the folder trusts it; a join file that brings a different one, or none where the folder has one, or one where the folder has none and already holds an endpoint or names servers in config.json, is refused, with or without --replace. The first join into an empty folder sets it; a folder that already holds an endpoint and has no ca.pem refuses a join file that brings one, with the same 'different ca' line, and a folder whose config.json already names servers but holds no endpoint refuses it with 'this folder has a server but no endpoint'. A JOIN FILE THAT HOLDS A SEED IS A SECRET FILE, and so is the file --key names: the file --key names is checked before it is read, and a join file is opened to see whether it holds a seed and then checked before anything is installed: it must be a plain file, owned by you, readable by you alone, or join refuses with the two cases above. A join file that holds only a user JWT is not checked for owner or mode, but any join file that is not a plain file (a directory, a FIFO, a device) gets the 'not a plain file of your own' line.
